q: The Dow rose 3.01% while the Nasdaq rose 6.51%. What best explains the gap?
options: The Dow was dragged down by a jump in the 10-year yield
The Nasdaq holds more consumer stocks that investors rushed into
The Nasdaq holds more AI-linked giants that Huang's return lifted most
The Dow holds more energy producers that fell with crude prices
explain: Nvidia and the companies that depend on its spending carry heavy weight in the Nasdaq, so the AI relief rally showed up there most. The 10-year yield rose only 1 basis point, so it wasn't a drag.

q: Kroger and Tyson Foods were among the S&P 500's biggest losers while Nvidia soared. What best explains that?
options: A jump in bond yields made grocery stocks less appealing
Investors sold steady defensive names to buy growth as fear faded
Higher oil prices raised their costs and hurt their profit outlook
Lawmakers started targeting food companies after Huang's return
explain: Investors had been hiding in safe stocks during the AI scare, so when fear faded they sold those shelters to buy tech. Oil actually fell 4.23% and the 10-year yield barely moved.

q: The BOJ chief has signaled a near-term hike. If the BOJ raises rates and narrows its gap with the Fed's 3.875%, what would USD/JPY, now 158.93, probably do?
options: Up
Down
explain: A higher Japanese rate makes holding yen more rewarding, so fewer traders sell yen for dollars and the yen strengthens. That pushes USD/JPY down.

q: Fed officials sound more hawkish about oil-driven inflation than traders expected. What would the 2-year yield, now 4.63%, probably do?
options: Up
Down
explain: The 2-year yield tracks expected Fed rates over the next two years, so tougher talk pushes it up. The San Francisco Fed research says the 10-year would react less because the inflation is supply-driven.

q: Reports of a formal SEC action against Nvidia hit while the VIX sits at 26.62. What would the VIX probably do?
options: Up
Down
explain: The rebound rests on the AI trade feeling safe again, so legal trouble at Nvidia would bring nerves back. Traders then pay more for protection and the VIX rises.

q: Put today's AI stock chain in the right cause-and-effect order.
items: S&P 500 posts its best day in over a year
explain: The personnel news came first, the AI-linked stocks reacted, their weight lifted the index, and the calmer market drained fear from the VIX.

q: Put today's oil chain in the right cause-and-effect order.
items: Gulf crude keeps flowing despite tanker attacks
WTI closes at its lowest since August
Gas prices and inflation pressure ease
Fed has less reason to hike
explain: Steady supply came first, so crude got cheaper, which eases inflation worries and gives the Fed a bit more room to wait.

q: The dollar index rose 0.49% to 104.32 mainly because investors reacted to the Democratic midterm rout.
options: True
False
explain: The midterms started the dollar conversation, but headlines credit hawkish Fed bets for today's gain.

q: The 2-year yield at 4.63% sitting well above the Fed's 3.875% rate suggests traders expect the Fed's next move to be a hike.
options: True
False
explain: Short-term yields follow expected policy rates, so a 2-year yield about 75 basis points above the Fed's rate means traders are betting on higher rates.

q: The St. Louis Fed found that the big AI spenders' debt compared with assets rose from about 25% in 2023 to nearly 30% in early 2026.
options: True
False
explain: The direction is backwards. Their ratio fell from nearly 30% to roughly 25%, so the spending has been funded mostly from profits.

q: Fed officials talked about higher rates over time, yet the 10-year yield rose only 1 basis point to 4.92%. Which explanation fits best?
options: Bond traders ignored the Fed because the stock rally absorbed all the buying
Williams said inflation will near 2% in 2027, which erased every hike bet
The 2-year yield fell enough to cancel out the rise in long-term yields
Oil-driven inflation is a supply problem, so Fed surprises reach long-term yields less
explain: The San Francisco Fed letter found Fed surprises pass through to longer yields mainly when inflation is demand-driven. Hike bets haven't disappeared, since the 2-year still sits well above the Fed's rate.

q: Cook warned that damaged infrastructure and low inventories could keep oil prices high for a long time. Why does that matter after WTI's 4.23% drop?
options: It means oil company stocks should fall more than crude itself
It suggests the relief could fade, so inflation worries might return
It shows Gulf tankers have stopped moving, which explains the drop
It means the Fed will cut rates now that oil is cheaper
explain: Today's drop came from steady flows, but Cook's point is that the underlying supply is still fragile. That means cheaper oil may not last, and neither would the relief for inflation.

q: The VIX fell 25.83% to 26.62. What does that say about the mood in the market?
options: Traders are buying more protection because the index rose so far
Traders expect smaller swings than before, but nerves are still high
Traders expect the S&P 500 to keep rising after such a big jump
Traders see volatility as gone now that the index has bounced back
explain: A falling VIX means traders expect calmer markets, so fear drained out. The level is still elevated, so the market hasn't fully relaxed.

q: Why does the gap between the Fed's 3.875% and the BOJ's 1.25% keep pressure on the yen?
options: Low Japanese rates push foreign investors to buy yen as a haven
Japan prints extra yen to buy dollars whenever rates diverge
Japan sells dollars each day until the rate gap closes by itself
Holding dollars pays more than holding yen, so traders sell yen
explain: A 2.625 percentage point gap rewards traders for holding dollars instead of yen, so they sell yen. Japan's intervention goes the other way, since it sells dollars to buy yen.

q: A New York Fed note says U.S. labor supply may soon shrink. Why does that matter for the Fed's energy inflation worry?
options: Fewer workers lets wages rise, so energy inflation could spread to services
Fewer workers means higher company profits, so stocks would rise
Fewer workers lowers growth, so the Fed would cut rates sooner
Fewer workers means less oil demand, so inflation would cool faster
explain: When employers compete for fewer workers, wages can rise, which can keep service prices climbing. That's exactly the leak into wages and services that central banks fear from the oil shock.

q: The ECB said it expects to publish the details of its new collateral requirements for tokenised assets in spring 2027, with implementation planned for June 2027.
options: True
False
explain: That's right, which is why the decision is slow plumbing news rather than something that moves rates or the euro today.
